t:
That section 136 of the Legislative Reorganization Act of 1946 (2 U.S.C. 190d), as amended by section 118 of the Legislative Reorganization Act of 1970 (84 Stat. 1156; Public Law 91–510), is amended to read as follows:

“legislative review by standing committees of the senate and house of representatives
“Sec. 136. 
(a) 
In order to assist the Congress in—

“(1) 
its analysis, appraisal, and evaluation of the application, administration, and execution of the laws enacted by the Congress, and


“(2) 
its formulation, consideration, and enactment of such modifications of or changes in those laws, and of such additional legislation, as may be necessary or appropriate,

each standing committee of the Senate, and the House of Representatives shall review and study, on a continuing basis, the application, administration, and execution of those laws, or parts of laws, the subject matter of which is within the jurisdiction of that committee.


“(b) 
In each odd-numbered year beginning on or after January 1, 1973, each standing committee of the Senate shall submit, not later than March 31, to the Senate, and each standing committee of the House shall submit, not later than January 2. to the House, a report on the activities of that committee under this section during the Congress ending at noon on January 3 of such year.


“(c) 
The preceding provisions of this section do not apply to the Committee on Appropriations of the Senate and the Committees on Appropriations. House Administration, Rules, and Standards of Official Conduct of the House.”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that "legislative review" and committee reports are a formal oversight process amounting to participation. Every actor here is inside the federal government: standing committees of Congress review how laws are administered and report to their own chambers. No state, tribe, expert, company, or member of the public is consulted, heard, or given a right to sue, so the section does not cross the federal boundary.
fable.s: each standing committee of the Senate, and the House of Representatives shall review and study, on a continuing basis, the application, administration, and execution of those laws

opus.w: The section requires congressional standing committees to keep reviewing how laws are carried out and to report to their own chambers. Congress and its committees are inside the federal government, so this is internal oversight, not participation by outsiders. The procedural language of review, study and reports may look like participation, but no state, expert, company or member of the public is brought into any decision.
opus.s: each standing committee of the Senate shall submit, not later than March 31, to the Senate, and each standing committee of the House shall submit, not later than January 2. to the House, a report on the activities of that committee under this section

qwen_chat.w: This section mandates that standing committees of the Senate and House of Representatives review and study laws. Since Congress and its committees are explicitly defined as being INSIDE the federal government, this activity is intra-governmental coordination and review. It does not involve consultation or coordination with any party outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or private entities).
qwen_chat.s: each standing committee of the Senate, and the House of Representatives shall review and study, on a continuing basis, the application, administration, and execution of those laws
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the committees are reviewing laws, they are participating in the legislative process. However, the definition explicitly states that Congress, its committees, and its members are INSIDE the federal government. Therefore, any interaction solely between these entities is intra-governmental and does not constitute "participation" as defined (which requires involvement of parties OUTSIDE the federal government).
